Essential reproducibility details are missing, including optimizer and learning rates, training schedule, preprocessing and resolution, U-Net configuration, target sequence construction, and baseline tuning. Target-cohort sizes and details of the private TBI cohort are also absent, while code is only promised after publication.
The method is formally described for binary foreground/background clicks, but its extension to the three-class fundus task is not specified clearly.

Dice is the only primary quality metric; boundary metrics and interaction time would be important for the paper's clinical-efficiency claims. The private clinical dataset also needs annotation, governance, consent or ethics, and demographic details.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: exploiting routine interactive corrections to adapt medical segmentation models under deployment-time distribution shift.
The proposed combination of post-interaction adaptation, mid-interaction adaptation, and a click-centered loss is conceptually coherent, simple, and computationally lightweight.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering fundus and MRI datasets, modality and pathology shifts, multiple click budgets, noisy clicks, sequence ordering, source-domain return, latency, and component-level ablations.

Reported gains over ICNN, IA+SA, and TSCA are large on difficult MRI shifts, and the paper is generally readable with helpful diagrams and pseudocode. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/r-3b30f255031c4d37/reviews/review-experiment-s31o3nur/call-a39a1925eb474c3fb6cf2e9919e89935/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The evaluation does not substantiate the strong clinical-practicality claims. Every interaction is generated by a ground-truth-aware simulator, with no clinician study or realistic stopping behavior. MRI evaluation uses only the 2D slice having the largest lesion area—an oracle, annotation-dependent selection that excludes negative slices, volumetric consistency, and much of the actual clinical task.

Reliability of the quantitative evidence is unclear. Main results lack variability, confidence intervals, or statistical tests despite random clicks and order-sensitive online adaptation; only one secondary ablation reports three seeds. Dataset sizes, target-image ordering, most splits, and the validation protocol are also incompletely specified.

There is a serious risk of target-test tuning. The main hyperparameters are described as selected in preliminary experiments, while sensitivity analyses use BRATS-T1 and WMH, but the paper does not identify an independent validation set or explain how target-domain hyperparameters were chosen without consulting evaluation data.

The central algorithm is underspecified and internally ambiguous. Mid-interaction adaptation marks the current-click prediction as no-gradient while optimizing the previous prediction, apparently requiring retention or recomputation of a graph across user interactions; neither is explained. It is also unclear whether pseudo-labels are hard masks or probabilities and where they are detached. Algorithm 2 appears to omit the initial localization click from the final training click set, contrary to the inference protocol.

Reproducibility is inadequate: optimizer, learning rates, preprocessing, spatial resolution, augmentation, U-Net configuration, thresholding, baseline hyperparameters, and several dataset details are absent, while code is only promised after publication. The private TBI dataset further prevents full reproduction.

The novelty is modest and weakly positioned relative to broader test-time adaptation, source-free adaptation, and pseudo-labeling literature. The entropy and cross-entropy comparisons are not well matched: they largely train a prediction toward its own current label, rather than testing the key re-prompting/distillation mechanism that uses the final refined mask.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on mean Dice. Boundary metrics, per-case failures, calibration, memory cost, equal-compute comparisons, and safety analyses are missing despite claims about accurate boundaries and real-world medical use.

The non-public clinical TBI data are presented without any statement about ethics approval, consent, anonymization, governance, or demographic composition. This is a material omission for a medically oriented submission. Overall, the promising results do not overcome the evaluation, reproducibility, positioning, and ethics deficiencies required for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/r-3b30f255031c4d37/reviews/review-experiment-mupz233w/call-7e4e0149993242d3b08ce99b428a6a37/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a clear, practically motivated framework combining mid-interaction adaptation, post-interaction adaptation, and a click-centered Gaussian loss.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering five fundus and four brain-MRI datasets with shifts across scanners, modalities, and pathologies. OAIMS consistently improves over the frozen model and key online-interactive baselines, with particularly large gains for difficult MRI shifts and early-click performance.

The paper includes substantial ablation and stress testing: individual loss terms and adaptation stages, Gaussian design choices, hyperparameters, different click budgets, mixed-domain streams, poor pseudo-labels, erroneous clicks, source-domain return, click efficiency, and runtime.
The method is simple and computationally inexpensive, and the algorithms, figures, and main experimental conclusions are generally easy to follow.
weaknesses: All interactions are simulated using dense ground truth to identify the largest erroneous component; there is no clinician study or alternative user simulator. Moreover, MRI evaluation uses only the ground-truth-selected slice with the largest lesion rather than complete 3D volumes. These choices substantially weaken claims about clinical practicality and real user effort.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the paper omits preprocessing and input resolution, detailed U-Net configuration, optimizer and learning rates, training schedules, adaptation hyperparameters beyond a few loss weights, sequence-order protocol, most dataset sample counts and splits, and baseline tuning details. Code and models are only promised after publication.

Most reported results are single point estimates despite randomness in click placement and target-image order, both of which can materially affect an online learner. Except for one ablation, there are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests.

The claimed model-agnostic generality is not demonstrated because adaptation is evaluated only with one U-Net-style backbone. Med-SA is merely frozen rather than equipped with comparable adaptation, and stronger contemporary interactive backbones are not tested.

The technical novelty is moderate: Gaussian-weighted local cross-entropy and pseudo-label fine-tuning are intuitive extensions of prior correction-based online learning. Some implementation-critical details are also ambiguous, including the gradient path through the stored previous prediction in mid-interaction adaptation and the very different effective weighting of CCG during pretraining versus adaptation.

The non-public TBI dataset lacks cohort size, provenance, access conditions, and ethics/consent or de-identification information. Given the medical setting, the absence of an explicit ethics and deployment-limitations discussion is notable. Overall, the empirical evidence supports a marginal accept, but not the paper's stronger claims of demonstrated clinical readiness or transformative impact.
